newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - New hippie movement takes root in Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New hippie movement takes root in Britain.

text.p: Forty-year-old Judy Jones admits she is part of the hippie movement of the 1990s.
"This doesn't mean I wander around with daisies in my tummy button or long hair," says Jones, who spends her spare time growing herbs at home in an affluent west London suburb.

But Jones, a freelance writer, belongs to a non-conformist fringe movement followed by thousands of other Britons who have bucked the trend and chosen to "downshift" -- quitting well-paid, prestigious, competitive careers in exchange for leisure time.
Social researcher Ian Christie says downshifting is a response to the hyper-competitive cut-throat 1990s that have forced many out of their jobs and alienated many employees.
"Downshifting is a symptom of a wider problem of insecurity," says Christie, associate director of the Henley Centre, a consumer consultancy company.

"It is being driven by burnout, by stress, by the fact that by definition, there are only a limited number of high-reward jobs around. A lot of people are going to be disappointed and disillusioned, and they are particularly vulnerable to the message of downshifting."
He says redundancies over the past five years have forced people to take a fresh look at their lives, and to re-examine what material assets and their families mean to them.
"Many of them may well decide they don't want to play the traditional career game any more," Christie said.
CASE HISTORY
Jones says she had worked for 20 years in smoke-filled newsrooms, rushing madly to meet deadlines, before she realised she had to get out of the rat race and opted for a voluntary redundancy scheme.
"I just felt I wanted a break. Downshifting is about slowing down. It's not retiring -- you carry on working, but the crucial difference is you feel more in control of your work," she said.
Jones now writes freelance and is working on a book, due to be released in February, called "Getting A Life: A Downshifter's Guide to Happier, Simpler Living."

"When you're in a well-paid job, you're under very strong pressure to conform, to keep up with the Joneses. Part of dwonshifting is realising that that attitude is irrelevant and obsolete. Downshifting forces you to realise that spending money doesn't necessarily make you happier," she said.
Jones says she sees it as a protest movement against the 1990s credo of over-consumption.
"Simple living as a movement has a very long pedigree. People have been wanting to slow down and get out of the hustle and bustle of life since time began," she says.
"The hippie movement was one expression of that desire and downshifting is the contemporary manifestation."
IDEA ACCEPTED IN UNITED STATES, BRITONS SLOW TO ADAPT
Christie says some 26 million Americans have already downshifted, but Britons have been slower to accept the idea, often regarding downshifters as eccentric.

"There is a problem with credibility, certainly with role models," he says. "It is peculiar to a lot of people to see Judy deliberately trading in her high-status job for more quality time. You have to be quite brave and self-possessed to do it."

Jones says she laughs when people ask her when she is getting a "real" job. "It helps if you don't much care what other people think about you. The more independent-minded you are, the easier downshifting is," she says.

Christie said he had found a very strong correlation between people who were concerned about the environment and "post-materialist" people, who have discovered that there is more to life than the acquisition of material goods.
Jones says women traditionally find it easier to downshift because they are better equipped to juggle their careers and families, and are more flexible about accepting low-paid work.

"Women are more enthusiastic, men are more hesitant and doubtful, perhaps because they are traditionally breadwinners and their sense of identity is more tied up with the trappings of a career -- the company car, the office politics -- while women much more tend to think it's a bit of a drag," she said.
According to Christie, Britain is starting to accept downshifting as a mainstream trend.
"We have now got to a point where an economy can do without so many people working, because the economy today is driven by new technology and globalisation, which displace people.
"And recession now hits the middle class and the service sector in a way it didn't before, exerting continuous pressure on manpower. That is a trend that won't go away," he says.
The average tenure of jobs held by men dropped to 73 months in 1996 from 99 months in 1975, according to a survey by the Henley Centre.
"So a space has been opened up where disillusionment and expression can breed, the social potential now exists for that to happen," Christie said.

In a 1996 Henley Centre poll, 28 percent of the people surveyed said they say would prefer more time off to more money in the future. A quarter said they would be willing to take on a lower paid job if it meant less stress and more free time.
But downshifting carries its own unique hazards, Jones says.

"It is potentially isolating," she says. "Some people do miss the company of colleagues. But one builds up networks of downshifters. If it takes off as a movement, support groups will emerge to counter this danger."
